text:
A: Hiya, lovely! I'm Ceri. Last one, is it?
B: Hello. Ioana. Yes, I think last.
A: Where are you, then?
B: London. Burnt Oak.
A: Pontypridd, me, South Wales. You must be shattered, all these calls. I'm knackered and I've only been talking.
B: Yes. I start work later, so now I am resting, sort of.
A: Oh, what's the work?
B: Cleaning. A primary school, evenings.
A: Oh, my mam did school canteen for years. Hard graft, that. Your back must be killing you.
B: Yes. The hall is the worst. Mopping the hall, it is very big.
A: I'd be crawling home. I was a hairdresser for twenty years, on my feet all day, and now I'm doing OT and I'm on my feet on placement. My legs have never had a day off, honestly.
B: You are a student now? This is good.
A: At forty-one, mind! Bit late.
B: I don't think it is late. I left university in Romania, literature. Sometimes I think I will go back. Open University, maybe. Art history.
A: Oh, you should! Do it! I did an Access course at thirty-eight, in the evenings, convinced I was thick, and I got through. Sorry, I'm bossing you now, I do that.
B: No, it's okay. Everybody tells me this. Then I look at the price.
A: The price, yeah. That's the bit. Dai's paying most of the mortgage while I do this and some days I feel awful about it. Sorry, that's a lot. Am I rambling?
B: No. My husband also, his work goes up and down. He is a plasterer. So I understand.
A: Ah, mine's a plumber! Self-employed. They'd get on, they'd just talk about vans.
B: Maybe, yes.
A: So art history, is that your thing then?
B: Yes. Museums. National Gallery, Tate. I go alone on my days off and stay for hours.
A: Oh, I love the National Museum in Cardiff. It's free, and they've got all these Impressionist ones, Monet and that, left by two sisters. And there's a big blue Renoir lady. I just sit in front of her.
B: The Davies sisters. Gwendoline and Margaret. I read about them. I want to go and see.
A: You know more about my museum than I do! Come down and I'll take you. It's only twenty minutes from Ponty on the train, when it runs.
B: What is the blue lady called?
A: La Parisienne. She's lush, all in this blue dress, like she's just come in and she's waiting for something.
B: I like paintings where somebody is waiting. You don't know for what.
A: Ooh, that's deep, that is. I just think, I want that dress. What do you cook, by the way? I was nosing at your kitchen in your photo.
B: Romanian food. Ciorbă, a sour soup, with lovage.
A: Ooh, I do cawl, my nan's recipe. Lamb and leeks and swede. Is yours with meat?
B: Sometimes. Meatballs, or chicken. My grandmother makes it best. She is old now, in Romania. I go every summer.
A: Aw. My nan's gone now, but every time I make the cawl I can sort of hear her telling me I've cut the leeks too
